title: The Ink Froze in the Pot

pages.text:
*The Owl Alley Sheet, No. 1. Today's news: the ink froze in the pot.*

On the coldest morning of the year, the ink in the Owl Alley print shop froze solid, and the first person to find out was Kichi, who put his brush into the pot and got it stuck there like a spoon in a bowl of ice.

"It is not my fault," Kichi announced to the whole room, which was already awake and already cold.

Haru had come down the ladder from the sleeping loft in her thickest kimono, with her breath smoking in front of her like a small private cloud. She looked at the pot. She looked at Kichi. She looked at the brush standing straight up out of the black ice like a tiny flagpole.

"That," she said, "is the truest thing I have ever heard you say."

Everybody laughed except Kichi, who was fourteen, gangly and the printer's apprentice, and who had not eaten yet, and so was not at his best.
pages.image: Inside a cold wooden print workshop at dawn, Kichi, a gangly 14-year-old boy in a moss-green short coat with a blue-and-white checked towel tied round his head, stares at a brush stuck upright in a pot of frozen black ink, while Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono with a vermilion cord in her small topknot bun, climbs down a wooden ladder from the loft with her breath smoking, blank paper sheets hanging on drying lines behind them.

pages.text:
Haru was eleven, and she had lived in this shop for every one of those years. She could have found her way through it with her eyes shut, and often did, on the mornings when the lamp had not been lit.

It was one long room. At one end was a low carving table, worn smooth and dark by her father's elbows. Along the walls stood shelves of cherry-wood blocks, each one carved with a picture or a page of words, each one waiting for its turn. Across the ceiling ran the drying lines, and from them hung sheets of paper, hundreds of them, pale as laundry. The whole place smelled of ink, wet paper and the sweet, clean curls of wood that lay like pale ribbons on the floor.

Her mother, Okiyo, was crouched by a small charcoal brazier with the ink pot in her hands, warming it slowly and laughing behind her sleeve at Kichi. Her father, Master Sota, sat at the carving table with a knife and did not look up at all. He carved the way other people breathe, steadily and without noticing.
pages.image: The long cozy room of a small family print shop at dawn: Father Sota, a broad calm man with a neat topknot, a white headband and a dark brown short work coat, carves a wooden block at a low table, while Mother Okiyo in a deep plum-purple kimono and a white apron warms an ink pot over a small glowing charcoal brazier, shelves of cherry-wood blocks along the walls, pale wood curls on the floor and blank paper sheets on drying lines overhead.

pages.text:
By the brazier, wrapped in a blue-grey quilted coat, sat her grandfather. Grandfather Tobei was thin and a little bent, with a bald head, a small white topknot and eyebrows so bushy that they seemed to have opinions of their own. He rubbed his right shoulder, as he did every cold morning.

"The best printer on Owl Alley," Haru's father liked to say, "and it is the shoulder that stopped him." Grandfather Tobei always answered that it was not the shoulder, it was sixty years of rubbing paper with a baren, and that any shoulder would have complained.

The baren was a flat round pad of coiled cord in a sheath of bamboo leaf. You pressed the back of a damp sheet of paper with it, hard and even, until the ink from the carved block sank into the paper. He was teaching Haru how to use it, a little each day.

"This shop makes calendars," he said now, holding out his hands to the fire. "It makes greeting sheets, notices, and pictures for children. And now and then, when something truly happens, it makes a small news sheet. Which is the one that gets us into trouble."

"Only a little trouble," said Haru.

"That," said Grandfather Tobei, "is how all trouble starts."
pages.image: Grandfather Tobei, a thin, slightly bent old man with a bald crown, a small white topknot, bushy white eyebrows and a soft blue-grey kimono with a folded towel around his neck, rubs his right shoulder beside a glowing charcoal brazier and holds a flat round baren of coiled cord, while Haru in her rust-orange kimono and indigo apron listens beside him in the warm workshop.

pages.text:
Haru had a job too, and she loved it more than anything. She was the shop's ears.

Every morning, after the first sheets were hung, she tied her little booklet to her belt. It was made of folded paper sewn with string, and the pages were a little grubby and a little ink-stained, because she wrote in it with a small brush. Then she went out to the well, the bathhouse steps and the noodle stall at the canal end, and listened. People talked in front of children as if they were furniture. She had heard about lost cats, a wedding, three arguments over a fence and one very interesting secret about a pickle.

She wrote down what she heard, and then she took the booklet home to her father, who read it slowly and asked the same question every single time.

"Did you see it with your own eyes?"

Sometimes the answer was yes. Often it was not. Then he shook his head and said the family rule, which was carved, in a way, into every one of them: "We print what happened. We do not print what people say happened."
pages.image: Haru, an eleven-year-old girl in a rust-orange kimono and indigo apron with a vermilion cord in her small topknot, stands at a stone well in a narrow wooden back alley in the cold morning writing carefully in a small booklet of folded paper on a string, while two neighbors in quilted coats talk close together nearby, tile roofs and a little steam rising behind them.

pages.text:
That morning she had nothing to tell him. No cat, no wedding, no pickle. But as she stood by the frozen pot with her hands tucked in her sleeves, a thought arrived.

"Father," she said. "We could put it on the sheet."

Master Sota looked up from his knife. "Put what?"

"The ink. The pot. The ink froze in the pot." She held up her booklet, with the words already written in small, stern brushstrokes. "It happened. I saw it with my own eyes. I saw Kichi's eyes too, and they were very wide."

There was a long silence, and then something happened at the corner of her father's mouth that in another man might have been called a smile. He drew a fresh block toward him and lifted his knife.

He had just made the first cut when a door slid open across the alley, and a big voice began to shout something, very loudly, about foxes.
pages.image: Father Sota, a broad calm man with a white headband and a dark brown short work coat, lifts a carving knife over a fresh wooden block at a low table with a small smile, while Haru in her rust-orange kimono and vermilion cord holds up her folded-paper booklet eagerly beside him, Kichi and Mother Okiyo watching, and a sliding door open to a bright cold alley behind them.
